name: Low-PUFA diet

lead: A low-PUFA diet avoids polyunsaturated fats from seed oils, nuts, seeds and fatty fish, favouring butter and coconut oil. It is most associated with followers of Ray Peat.
PUFAs do oxidise more easily than other fats in oils, but no trials have tested avoiding them for appearance or metabolic aims.

paras: Followers say PUFAs oxidise and burden metabolism. Chemistry supports that PUFAs are more oxidation-prone; the health consequences of normal intake are debated.

Linoleic and alpha-linolenic acids are essential nutrients and DHA supports brain and retinal function, so reference sources note the need for some intake. No specific harms of low-PUFA eating were identified in the sources.

lead: A low-PUFA diet is an eating pattern that minimises polyunsaturated fatty acids, found in vegetable seed oils, nuts, seeds and fatty fish. In online metabolism and appearance circles it is most associated with the Ray Peat diet, whose followers say PUFAs are unstable, oxidise easily and burden metabolism.

Chemically, PUFAs are more prone to lipid peroxidation and rancidity than saturated or monounsaturated fats.[1] Public health guidance generally treats unsaturated fats as the preferred fats, and omega-3 and omega-6 acids are essential nutrients.[1] The sources reviewed contain no clinical trials of deliberately minimising PUFA for appearance or metabolic goals.
infobox: Seed oils, nuts, seeds, fatty fish (per followers)

paras: Followers cite PUFAs' low melting point and chemical instability, saying they oxidise, turn rancid and produce toxic by-products. Their list of foods to limit includes nuts, seeds, fatty fish and vegetable, canola and corn oils, with coconut oil and butter favoured instead.

Chemistry reference material confirms that PUFAs are much more susceptible to peroxidation than other fats because of weak allylic hydrogen bonds, which shortens the shelf life of oils.[1] Whether this translates to harm from normal dietary intake is a separate question.

Reference summaries describe linoleic acid and alpha-linolenic acid as essential fatty acids, and DHA as important for brain and retinal function.[1] A Cochrane review of omega-3 supplements found little or no effect on mortality or cardiovascular health, and a re-analysis of 1960s-70s trial data linking linoleic acid substitution to higher mortality has been disputed by many scientists.[1]

Studies in the literature on PUFA and oxidative stress include a human crossover study comparing diets providing 5% and 15% of energy from PUFA on oxidative stress indices.[2] Other work, mostly in animals, examines n-6 to n-3 ratios, lipid levels and tumour growth, and is not specific to a low-PUFA lifestyle.[3]
No studies found of a low-PUFA diet used for appearance or metabolic-rate goals. Related human research has compared fixed PUFA levels on oxidative stress markers, in a small crossover design.[2]

lore.intro: Low-PUFA eating is discussed on looksmax.org mainly as part of Ray Peat-inspired diets.

claims.claim: PUFAs oxidise and become toxic in the body, so should be minimised
